content: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a condition that affects 8% to 13% of women of reproductive age and is associated with both reproductive and metabolic dysfunction. Obesity exacerbates the symptoms of PCOS, and weight management—whether through weight loss, maintenance, or prevention of further weight gain—is considered a primary treatment approach. This is best achieved through lifestyle modifications that include dietary changes, physical activity, and behavioral interventions. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of lifestyle interventions in improving reproductive outcomes, anthropometric measures (such as weight and body composition), metabolic parameters, and quality of life in women with PCOS. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecology and Fertility Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL, and AMED, up until March 2018. Additional sources such as trial registries, conference abstracts, relevant journals, and grey literature were also reviewed, with no restrictions on language. The study included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared lifestyle interventions—such as diet, exercise, behavioral therapy, or a combination of these—to minimal or no treatment in women with PCOS. Two independent reviewers selected the trials, assessed the quality of evidence and risk of bias, and extracted data. The primary outcomes of interest were live birth, miscarriage, and pregnancy, while secondary outcomes included menstrual regularity, weight, body mass index (BMI), and metabolic parameters. Meta-analyses were conducted using inverse variance and fixed-effect models, with dichotomous outcomes reported as odds ratios and continuous outcomes as mean differences (MD) or standardized mean differences (SMD). Fifteen studies involving 498 participants were included in the analysis. Ten studies compared physical activity to minimal dietary and behavioral interventions or no intervention, while five studies evaluated combined dietary, exercise, and behavioral interventions against minimal intervention. One study assessed behavioral intervention alone compared to minimal intervention. The risk of bias varied across studies: eight studies had adequate sequence generation, seven had adequate blinding of clinicians or outcome assessors, seven had adequate allocation concealment, six had complete outcome data, and six were free of selective reporting. None of the included studies assessed the primary fertility outcomes of live birth or miscarriage. Additionally, no studies reported on the secondary reproductive outcome of menstrual regularity as defined in this review. However, lifestyle interventions may improve a secondary endocrine reproductive outcome, the free androgen index (FAI), with a mean difference of -1.11 (95% confidence interval [CI] -1.96 to -0.26) based on six RCTs involving 204 participants. The evidence for this outcome was of low quality and showed high heterogeneity (I² = 71%). Lifestyle interventions may also lead to reductions in weight, with a mean difference of -1.68 kg (95% CI -2.66 to -0.70) based on nine RCTs involving 353 participants. Similarly, BMI may be reduced by -0.34 kg/m² (95% CI -0.68 to -0.01) based on 12 RCTs involving 434 participants. Both outcomes were supported by low-quality evidence, with moderate heterogeneity for weight (I² = 47%) and no heterogeneity for BMI (I² = 0%). The effect of lifestyle interventions on glucose tolerance, as measured by glucose outcomes in an oral glucose tolerance test, remains uncertain. The standardized mean difference was -0.02 (95% CI -0.38 to 0.33) based on three RCTs involving 121 participants, with low-quality evidence and no heterogeneity (I² = 0%). In conclusion, lifestyle interventions may improve the free androgen index (FAI), weight, and BMI in women with PCOS. However, the effect of these interventions on glucose tolerance is uncertain. Importantly, no studies included in this review evaluated the impact of lifestyle interventions on live birth, miscarriage, or menstrual regularity. The overall quality of evidence was low, primarily due to high or unclear risk of bias in most studies and significant heterogeneity in the FAI outcome.
